### Part A - Creating Data Frames

<br>

```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c("20", "21", "19", "22", "20")
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

<br>

```{r}
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
print(students)
```

<br>

```{r}
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```

<br>

```{r}
courses <- data.frame(
course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
units = c(3, 3, 2),
intstructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
```

<br>

##### Question #1:

- You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline.
- Both approaches produce the same kind of object.

```{r}
# A data frame is a table, so every column must have the same number of values. If one column has 5 values and another has 3, some cells would be empty. That’s why data.frame() stops with an error like arguments imply differing number of rows: 5, 3. The only exception is when the shorter column fits evenly into the longer one, like a single value that gets repeated.
```

<br> 

##### Question #2:

- A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.
- Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

```{r}

# A list holds elements of any type, and each element is independent of the others. A data frame is a list whose elements are the columns, with the added rule that they must all have the same length. Each column is an atomic vector, and a vector can hold only one type, because R coerces mixed values to a single type (c(1, "a", TRUE) becomes all character). So a column holds one type, while the data frame as a whole can mix types across columns, just as a list can hold different types in different elements.

```

##### Question #3:

- students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects.

- Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.


```{r}
class(students$age)
class(students["age"])

# Single brackets [ ] give you a smaller piece of the same type, so students["age"] is still a data frame with one column. Double brackets [[ ]] and $ pull out the content itself, so students$age is just the plain vector of ages.
```

<br>

##### Question #4:

- In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows.

- What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

```{r}
# students$passed == TRUE gives TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE, and students$age > 19 gives TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE. With &, R checks each position and keeps it only if both are TRUE, so the result is TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE. R then keeps the rows marked TRUE. With |, a position only needs one TRUE, so the result is TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE, which also includes Eli (age 20, did not pass). & is stricter and | gives more rows.

# With &, a row must pass both conditions. With |, it only needs to pass one, so you get more rows back. For example, age > 20 & score > 90 gives only older students with high scores, while age > 20 | score > 90 also includes anyone who meets just one of the two.
```

##### Question #5:

- Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name).
- Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

```{r}
# For a number column like age, the summary shows the lowest and highest values, the middle value, the average, and the values a quarter and three-quarters of the way through the data. For a true or false column like passed, it counts how many are false and how many are TRUE. For a text column like name, it only shows how many values there are, the type of data, and the mode, because there is nothing to calculate.
```

<br>

##### Question #6:

- str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information.

- Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

```{r}
# str() shows how your data is set up: how many rows and columns, what type each column is, and a few sample values. Use it right after you load or create data to make sure every column has the right type. summary() shows what the values look like, such as the lowest, highest, and average, or how many are TRUE and FALSE. Use it once you know the setup and want to understand the data, like the usual age or how many passed.
```


<br>

```{r}
students$passed <- NULL
```

<br>

```{r}
students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

<br>

##### Question #7:

- After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)?

- Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

```{r}
# It would not cause an error. students$passed is now NULL, so the check gives an empty result, and the filter returns a table with no rows (the column names still show). This is risky because the code runs fine but looks like nobody passed. That’s why you should check your data with names() or str() after each change, so later code doesn’t use columns that were removed.
```

<br>

##### Question #8:

- order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions.

- Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

```{r}
# students$age is 20 21 19 22 20, and order() gives the row numbers that would line up those ages from smallest to biggest: 3 1 5 2 4. So row 3 (age 19) comes first, then row 1, then row 5, and so on, and the two 20s stay in the same order as before. students[c(3, 1, 5, 2, 4), ] uses those numbers to choose the rows, and the empty space after the comma means “all columns.” R moves each whole row into that order, so name, age, and year_level stay together and only the order of the rows changes.
```

### Part E - Critical Thinking Challenge

<br>

```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)
```

```{r}
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
```

<br>

```{r}
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```

<br>

##### Question #9:

- Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”

- Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

```{r}
# First, I would add a drop column (grades$drop <- grades$midterm - grades$final) and a remarks column based on the average, so each student is marked Passed or Failed. Then I would sort by drop and by midterm with order() and check which list has the Failed students near the top. In this data, Eli has the lowest midterm (70) and is the only one who fails, while Dex, the only student whose score dropped, still passed. So a low midterm looks like the bigger factor, though five students are too few to be sure.
```


### Conclusion:

```{r}
# A data frame is a table in R where each column is a vector and each row is one record. It is really a list of vectors that all have the same length, so each column holds one type of data, but different columns can hold different types. You can use list tools like $ and [[ ]] to get a column, and matrix-style tools like [row, column] to get rows and values. Because it handles this mix of data types in one table, it is R’s go-to structure for real-world data like surveys or student records, where names, numbers, and yes/no values sit side by side.
```
